title: Why QR Codes Have Become a Phishing Tool
summary: QR code scams in Malaysia rose from 223 cases in 2023 to 5,907 in 2025. How QR phishing works, why people fall for it, and how to protect yourself.
body:
QR codes are now part of daily life in Malaysia. We scan them to pay with DuitNow QR, to pay for parking, to open a restaurant menu or to register for an event. That habit is exactly what makes them useful to scammers.

## From the factory floor to everyday payments

The QR (Quick Response) code was invented in 1994 by DENSO WAVE in Japan, originally to track automotive parts during manufacturing [1]. It was designed to be read regardless of orientation, and to stay readable even when part of the code is damaged or covered [2]. The same strengths help attackers. A QR code can be printed, stuck on a wall or sent in an email, and it will still scan.

## What QR phishing is

QR phishing, often called quishing, replaces an ordinary link with a QR code. Scanning the code opens a fake website that asks for login or banking details, or leads to malware that gives a criminal access to the phone [4]. The core problem is simple: people cannot read a QR code. A text link can be checked before it is clicked, but a QR code reveals nothing about where it leads until it has been scanned.

The threat is not new. In 2013, researchers at Carnegie Mellon University studied what they called QRishing [2]. They put up posters with QR codes in 139 locations, and over four weeks the codes were scanned by 225 people who went on to visit the linked websites. Their survey suggested that curiosity is the biggest reason people scan. In a smaller observation experiment, 85% of the people who scanned a code went on to open the link.

## The numbers in Malaysia

According to the Bukit Aman Commercial Crime Investigation Department (CCID), Malaysia recorded 11,919 QR code scam cases with losses of RM80.86 million between January 2023 and June 2026 [3]:

- 2023: 223 cases, RM4.59 million in losses
- 2024: 655 cases, RM6.76 million
- 2025: 5,907 cases, RM40.85 million
- January to June 2026: 5,134 cases, RM28.67 million

The number of cases in 2025 was more than 26 times the number in 2023, and the first six months of 2026 came close to the total for the whole of 2025.

## Common tactics

- A fake QR code sticker placed over a genuine one, for example on a parking meter [4][5].
- A QR code in an email or text message you were not expecting, often urging you to act immediately [5].
- Urgent requests for payment, refunds, prizes or account verification that come with a QR code [3].
- A message claiming that a payment failed and can only be completed by scanning a QR code [4].
- QR codes that lead to app downloads or carry malware [4].

## How to protect yourself

- After scanning, check the web address before you open it, and make sure it is the site you expected [4][5].
- Look closely at physical QR codes for a sticker placed on top of the original [4].
- Do not scan QR codes in emails or text messages you were not expecting, especially codes sent by people you do not know [3][5].
- Do not download apps through a QR code. Use your phone's official app store [4].
- Avoid making payments on a site opened from a QR code. Type in an address you know and trust instead [4].
- Keep your phone's operating system up to date, and protect your accounts with strong passwords and multi-factor authentication [5].
- In Malaysia, if you suspect a scam or have lost money, call the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) at 997 immediately. You can also check bank accounts, phone numbers and company names on the CCID SemakMule portal [6].

## Why this matters to my research

QR phishing is the focus of my PhD research at the School of Computing, Universiti Utara Malaysia. Most of the advice above depends on people checking every scan themselves, and the Malaysian figures show how often that fails. I will share more about the research here as the work progresses.

title: QR Codes in Work Email: How Quishing Gets Past the Filters
summary: In 2026, attackers hid QR codes in salary letters and fake invitations to get past email security. Two recent cases, what the numbers show, and what organizations can do.
body:
Most of us have learned to hover over a link before clicking it. A QR code gives us nothing to hover over. When one arrives in a work email, attached to what looks like a salary letter or a meeting invitation, the only way to see where it leads is to scan it, usually with a personal phone. Attackers know this, and in 2026 they used it against organisations around the world.

## Why a QR code slips past email security

Email security tools are good at checking links written as text. A QR code is a picture. The FBI explains that quishing campaigns commonly deliver QR images as email attachments or embedded graphics, which lets them avoid URL inspection, rewriting and sandboxing [2]. The QR code also forces the victim to move from a managed work computer to a mobile device, which usually sits outside the organisation's endpoint detection and network monitoring [2].

Microsoft's data shows where attackers are hiding the codes. In July and August 2026, 78% of the QR code attacks it observed were carried in PDF attachments, falling to 61% in September [1].

## Case 1: the "Salary Review" campaign

On 19 August 2026, Microsoft observed a campaign that reached more than 10,000 users in more than 4,800 organisations, almost all in the United States [1]. About 72.1% of the targets were in professional services. The emails used the subject "Salary Review" and carried a Word attachment named "Your-Q3-Compensation-Summary.docx" with a QR code inside [1].

Scanning the code led to a fake OneDrive sign-in page that used a technique called device code phishing [1]. The lure was well chosen. Few employees ignore a message about their pay.

## Case 2: QR codes in state-sponsored spear phishing

In January 2026, the FBI warned that Kimsuky, a North Korean state-sponsored group, had been sending QR codes in spear-phishing emails to think tanks, academic institutions and government bodies [2]. In May and June 2025, the group posed as a foreign adviser, an embassy employee and a think tank employee. One email invited a strategic advisory firm to a conference that did not exist, and its QR code led to a fake Google login page [2].

The FBI also describes what happens after the scan. Victims pass through redirectors that collect details such as the phone's operating system, IP address and screen size, then see a mobile-friendly login page imitating Microsoft 365, Okta or a VPN portal [2]. The attackers then steal session tokens, which lets them bypass multi-factor authentication without triggering the usual "MFA failed" alerts [2].

## Fewer attacks, sharper attacks

The overall volume is falling. Microsoft counted about 12.1 million QR code phishing attacks in the third quarter of 2026, 67% fewer than in the second quarter, and monthly volume was 86% below its March peak [1]. That is welcome, but the two cases above show that the attacks that remain are targeted and well disguised.

People are also part of the gap. In a small observational study of 20 participants in Japan, presented at SOUPS 2026, almost all participants skipped checking the destination after scanning a QR code [3]. The researchers also found that awareness of quishing lagged well behind awareness of ordinary phishing [3].

## What organisations and staff can do

The FBI recommends a layered approach [2]:

- Teach staff the risks of scanning unsolicited QR codes, whether they arrive by email, letter, flyer or packaging.
- Verify a QR code through a second channel, such as contacting the sender directly, before entering a password or downloading a file.
- Set up a clear way to report suspicious QR codes.
- Use mobile device management or endpoint security that can check QR-linked addresses before they open.
- Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication for remote access and sensitive systems.
- Log and monitor sign-ins and network activity after QR code scans to spot anything unusual.

For individuals in Malaysia, the same caution applies to payments. The police have reminded the public that a person receiving a DuitNow QR payment never needs to scan a code sent by the payer [4]. If you suspect a scam, call the National Scam Response Centre at 997 [4].

## Why this matters to my research

QR phishing is the focus of my PhD research at the School of Computing, Universiti Utara Malaysia. These cases show why detection cannot rely only on checking links in email text and why people need clear help at the moment they scan.
